A Day for Songs and Contests.

The Phaeacian Assembly and the Ship.
To assembly, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians!
Come and learn of the stranger newly come to the wise king's house —
a man like the deathless gods to look on!
Athena makes Odysseus appear larger and more impressive as he enters.
Draw a black ship down to the bright sea, and let fifty-two picked youths make her ready for the voyage.
The rest of you, lords, come to my hall —

And summon Demodocus, for to him the god has given song beyond all others.
The people ready the vessel while the palace fills for celebration.

scenes.title: The Athletic Challenge
scenes.card: At the games a young man named Euryalus mocks the stranger, and Odysseus answers by throwing a discus farther than anyone.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Athletic Challenge.
The youths of Phaeacia rise up:
they run and the dust hangs over the plain, they wrestle, they leap, they hurl the discus,
they trade blows in boxing.
Laodamas invites Odysseus.
Euryalus insults him as a merchant without athletic skill.
That was badly spoken, young man, and it stings me to my feet.
See where the stone flew —
past every mark of yours, and I threw it clothed and weary.
Now let any Phaeacian but Laodamas, my host's son, come and try me —
boxing, wrestling, or the race, I refuse no one.
Alcinous calms the confrontation and shifts the display toward dance and song.

scenes.title: The Dance and the Net of Hephaestus
scenes.card: Demodocus sings of two gods caught in a net, dancers perform, and Euryalus apologizes with the gift of a sword.

subs.text: Scene four.
The Dance and the Net of Hephaestus.
Hear now how Ares and golden Aphrodite lay together in secret,
and how the lame smith Hephaestus forged a net fine as spider-thread that no eye could see,
and caught the lovers fast in his own bed till all the gods stood laughing at the door.
Phaeacian dancers perform a ball dance with precise leaps and exchanges.
Alcinous, you boasted your dancers were the best beneath the sun, and here the boast stands proved.
Wonder takes me as I watch —
their feet flash and my eyes cannot follow.
The nobles offer gifts.
Farewell, father stranger —
if a harsh word was spoken, let the storm winds snatch it up and carry it away.
Take this sword of bronze, silver on the hilt, the sheath new-carved ivory,
and may the gods grant you your home and your wife.

captain.asks: Keep a tableau behind the singer with Odysseus listening, so the tale of the net and the dance on the ground mirror each other.
diagnosis: The singer is never seen: audiences listen to nothing, so the mise en abyme loses its centre.
The dances themselves are strong, ring, leap and festival crowd, but saturated colour rows wait in the alternatives to break the bw.

scenes.title: The Trojan Horse Song and the Name
scenes.card: Odysseus asks for the song of the wooden horse, weeps again, and the king finally demands to know his name and story.

subs.text: Scene five.
The Trojan Horse Song and the Name.
Demodocus, above all mortals I honor you —
the Muse taught you, surely, or Apollo, for you sing the Achaeans' fate as though you stood among them.
Take this cut of honor from my own portion.
Now shift your ground and sing the wooden horse, the trap Epeius built with Athena,
that noble Odysseus led up into Troy filled with fighting men.
Sing now:
the Greeks' emergence, the sack, and Odysseus's attack on Deiphobus's house.
Odysseus weeps like a captive woman over a fallen husband.
Stop the lyre, Demodocus —
not all here take joy of it, for since the song began our guest has not once left off weeping.
Now, stranger, hide it no longer:
tell me the name your father and mother called you, and your land and your city.
And say why you weep at the doom of the Argives and Troy —
did some kinsman fall there, or a comrade dear as a brother?
You ask, king, and I will tell you all of it —
though the telling opens every wound.

sign.name: Mise en abyme
sign.operation: Frame the singer with a tableau of the horse behind him in the lamplight while Odysseus listens in the foreground; the told Troy and the listening hall share the image.

scenes.world: The same lamplit banquet hall at night, deep shadows and flickering oil lamps, silent costume-drama staging.

captain.asks: Frame the singer with a tableau of the horse behind him while Odysseus weeps in the foreground, so sung Troy and the listening hall share one lamplit image.
diagnosis: The two layers never coexist: Troy (fire, gate) and the hall (tuxedo tables) alternate as separate films, no tableau holds both.
The weeping, the scene's hinge, is played by a melodrama heroine in a forest and a fallen white shape; the man never appears.
Night-black and lamp-glow hold a shared palette, which keeps a stranger in one mood if not one place.

prologue: The Phaeacians hold a day of feasting, games, and songs for their unknown guest. A blind singer performs stories of the war at Troy, and some of them are about Odysseus himself. The guest's tears begin to give him away.
